abstract.p: Highway operators increasingly hold two complementary data sources: electronic toll collection (ETC) gantry records, which give vehicle travel times over intervals several kilometres long, and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) video, which resolves traffic in detail but only over short, intermittently observed road sections. Combining them is difficult because an interval travel time does not reveal where along the interval vehicles slowed down, and because the reliability of video-derived measurements varies with coverage and tracking conditions. This study develops a spatially aware, quality-adaptive traffic fusion (SQA-TF) method that estimates flow, space-mean speed and density on a common grid of road cells. ETC travel times were modelled as path constraints on the speeds of all cells within each gantry interval, with time-overlap weights for trips spanning several time windows. UAV measurements entered the estimation only in covered cells, and every residual was weighted by a quality score. A fundamental-relation penalty and a spatiotemporal smoothness penalty completed the objective. The method was evaluated with synthetic traffic states and synthetic observations on a corridor configured as a 147 km highway with 23 ETC gantries, using 200 independent simulation trials. Across the six error metrics (mean absolute error and root mean square error, i.e., MAE and RMSE of the three variables), SQA-TF reduced errors by 21.0–23.5% relative to the same model with fixed weights, by 29.4–32.9% relative to fixed-weight fusion, and by 41.2–43.4% relative to estimation from UAV data alone. The largest reconstruction errors of single-source estimation and linear interpolation occurred in the most congested section, whereas SQA-TF errors remained comparatively uniform along the corridor. These results show, under controlled conditions, that treating ETC data as interval constraints and weighting observations by quality yields more accurate corridor-wide estimates than fixed-weight fusion; validation with field data is still required before operational use.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Operational management of long highway corridors depends on knowing traffic flow, speed, and density at a spatial resolution fine enough to locate congestion, yet these variables are measured directly at only a small number of locations. Traffic state estimation (TSE) addresses this gap by inferring the full space–time field of traffic variables from sparse and noisy observations [1]. On Chinese expressways, two data sources have become available on a scale that makes corridor-wide estimation practical. Electronic toll collection (ETC) gantries record anonymised passage events at intervals of several kilometres, from which individual travel times between successive gantries can be derived [2]. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), operated either at fixed hovering positions or on inspection flights, provide video from which vehicle trajectories and local traffic parameters can be extracted [3], [4]. The two sources complement each other: ETC covers the entire corridor but resolves it only at interval level, whereas UAV video resolves individual cells but only where and when a drone is flying.

Fusing these sources raises three difficulties. First, an inter-gantry travel time integrates the speeds of all road cells along the interval, so dividing interval length by travel time gives an average that can coincide with very different local speed profiles. Assigning that average to every cell flattens congestion that may occupy only a fraction of the interval. Second, the observations are asynchronous and spatially mismatched: gantry intervals do not coincide with UAV footprints, and a single trip may span several estimation time windows. Third, the reliability of UAV measurements changes with flight geometry, occlusion, and tracking continuity, and ETC travel-time samples vary in size and dispersion between intervals and periods. A fusion scheme with fixed weights cannot respond to these changes.

This study develops and evaluates a method, termed spatially aware, quality-adaptive traffic fusion (SQA-TF), that addresses the three difficulties within a single optimisation problem. The method places both data sources on a common grid of road cells derived from the corridor topology, represents each ETC travel time as a constraint on the sum of cell traversal times along its interval, admits UAV measurements only in covered cells, and weights every observation residual by a quality score. A soft fundamental-relation penalty and a spatiotemporal smoothness penalty regularise the estimate in cells without direct observations. The evaluation reported here uses synthetic traffic states and synthetic observations on a corridor configured as a 147 km highway with 23 ETC gantries. This design allows errors to be computed against known reference states in every cell, including those never observed by a UAV.

The contributions of the study are as follows. (i) An estimation formulation is presented in which ETC travel times act as interval-level path constraints with time-overlap weighting, so that local speed variations within an interval are inferred from UAV observations and regularisation rather than imposed by the interval average. (ii) Observation residuals are weighted by quality scores; in the simulation, this weighting reduced all six error metrics by 21.0–23.5% relative to an otherwise identical model with fixed weights. (iii) A corridor-scale simulation study compares the method with single-source estimation, linear interpolation and fixed-weight fusion, and analyses where along the corridor and in which traffic regimes the improvements arise.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 formulates the estimation problem and presents SQA-TF. Section 4 describes the simulation design, and Section 5 reports the results. Section 6 discusses the findings and their limits, and Section 7 concludes the paper.

sec.title: 2.1. Model-based and data-driven traffic state estimation
sec.p: The Lighthill–Whitham–Richards (LWR) model describes how traffic density disturbances propagate along a road [5], [6]. The cell transmission model gives a discrete representation of that process [7]. Wang and Papageorgiou [8] coupled freeway dynamics to an extended Kalman filter to estimate densities and speeds from detector measurements. Mobile observations provide a different constraint. Rastogi et al. [9] used partial trajectories from camera-equipped probe vehicles to calibrate a cell model and infer densities outside the camera view. Wu et al. [10] reconstructed traffic conditions from vehicle trajectories with an anisotropic Gaussian process whose correlation structure follows the direction of traffic waves.

Physics-informed estimators impose structure where measurements are sparse. Huang and Agarwal [11] examined the use of the Lighthill–Whitham–Richards (LWR) model and cell transmission models in neural-network training. Subsequent studies compared physical models on freeways [12], fitted traffic-flow parameters within a computational graph [13], and examined reconstruction under sparse freeway observations [14]. Wang et al. [15] allowed scatter in the flow–density relation through a stochastic fundamental diagram. In the present setting, a separate observation model is needed for ETC: a vehicle can spend the same total time in a gantry interval under quite different local speed profiles.

sec.title: 2.2. Fusion of local measurements with travel-time data
sec.p: Data fusion in intelligent transportation systems has long been motivated by the complementary strengths of different sensors [16]. Two families of methods are directly relevant here. Adaptive smoothing reconstructs space–time speed fields by filtering detector data along the characteristic directions of free and congested traffic; Treiber et al. [17] generalised it to fuse stationary detectors with floating-car data. Van Lint and Hoogendoorn [18] proposed a fusion method that accepts data of arbitrary spatial and temporal structure, including travel times from automatic vehicle identification, provided that free-flowing and congested regimes can be distinguished. Kessler et al. [19] compared such methods on loop, floating-car, and Bluetooth data from a congested German freeway and found that travel-time data improved speed reconstruction only when they were integrated as travel times rather than as local speeds. This finding supports the treatment of interval data as path constraints.

ETC records play the role of automatic vehicle identification data on Chinese expressways. Jiang et al. [20] estimated traffic states and emissions on urban expressways from heterogeneous data. Zhang et al. [21] formulated freeway TSE as a data-driven optimisation that fuses ETC and detector data, and Huang et al. [22] combined ETC and sensor data in a predict-then-optimise framework that retrieves recurrent traffic patterns. Wang et al. reviewed ETC-based traffic sensing and noted the growing use of ETC alongside floating-car and video data [2]. In these studies, the local data source is a fixed detector with continuous coverage and stable reliability. When the local source is a UAV, coverage is intermittent and measurement quality changes from one flight segment to the next, so the relative influence of local and interval data should vary across the space–time grid.

sec.title: 2.3. Unmanned aerial vehicle-based traffic observation
sec.p: Drone studies provide both vehicle trajectories and evidence about their accuracy. CitySim provides trajectories for safety analysis across a range of road layouts [23]. Berghaus et al. [24] documented trajectory fragmentation on a highway section with ramps and congestion, while Fonod et al. [25] addressed camera stabilisation and georeferencing across drone views. These distinctions matter for traffic estimation: a fragmented track may still register a vehicle passage, whereas a position error can assign that vehicle to the wrong road cell. Methods for recovering traffic parameters from aerial footage [3], [4] therefore supply local observations whose accuracy depends on the measurement and the camera view.

Even with accurate extraction, a UAV observes only the section within its field of view and only for the duration of a flight. Measurement errors grow with occlusion, perspective distortion, motion blur and, for moving platforms, imperfect camera-motion compensation. Cells outside the footprint carry no visual information and must not be treated as zero-traffic observations. Corridor-wide estimation therefore requires UAV data to be combined with a source that covers the remaining cells, and the combination should reflect how reliable each UAV measurement is. The method in Section 3 is designed around these requirements: interval constraints from ETC records supply corridor coverage, quality-weighted UAV residuals supply local detail, and physical regularisation links the two.

sec.title: 4.1. Corridor and synthetic data
sec.p: The simulation corridor reproduces the geometry of a 147 km highway section with 23 ETC gantries, giving 22 gantry intervals with a mean length of about 6.7 km. The corridor was divided into 294 cells of 500 m, and the time window was 5 min. Synthetic reference states of flow, speed and density were specified for every cell and window, and synthetic UAV observations and synthetic ETC travel-time records were generated from them. The reference field contains three congested sections, centred near km 32, km 77, and km 119; the second is the longest and most severe, with mean speeds falling to about 53 km/h (Figure 2). At the representative cell examined in Section 5.3, the reference speed falls from about 90–100 km/h to about 50 km/h during a congestion episode and then recovers (Figure 3). UAV observations were available for a subset of cells, so that every method had to infer the state of unobserved cells.

Speed estimates at a representative cell over 200 time windows

sec.p: Each method was evaluated in 200 independent simulation trials. The data of each trial were split into training, validation, and test portions in the proportions 60%, 20%, and 20% by contiguous time periods rather than by randomly sampled windows, which limits information leakage between portions. Coefficients were selected on the validation portion, and all reported errors were computed on the test portion against the synthetic reference states. Because the data are synthetic, the evaluation measures the estimation method itself; errors introduced by vehicle detection, tracking, and ETC record matching in field data are represented only to the extent that they are reproduced by the synthetic observation errors.

sec.title: 4.2. Comparison methods
sec.p: Six methods were compared (Table 2). UAV-only and ETC-only use a single source on the same grid; ETC-only estimates cell states from the travel-time model of Section 3.2 and does not assign interval-average speeds to cells. Linear interpolation fills unobserved cells from the states of observed cells. Fixed-weight fusion combines UAV observations and ETC travel-time constraints with constant weights. SQA-TF without quality adaptation retains the topology-based mapping, temporal association, and flow-consistency term of SQA-TF but replaces the quality scores with fixed weights; comparing it with the full model isolates the effect of quality weighting. Fixed weights were set without using test data. Within each trial, all six methods were applied to the same test observations, so differences between them, including the difference between SQA-TF and its fixed-weight variant, reflect the estimation methods rather than the data. In the ETC-only case, travel time constrains speed along a path. Even if speed were known exactly, the flow–density relation would still admit multiple flow and density pairs. The corresponding errors in Table 3 describe model-dependent reconstructions.

sec.title: 5.1. Overall accuracy
sec.p: Table 3 lists the errors of all six methods. SQA-TF gave the lowest MAE and RMSE for every variable, with a flow MAE of 86.42 veh/h/lane, a speed MAE of 4.12 km/h and a density MAE of 2.74 veh/km/lane. The ranking of the methods was the same for all six metrics: ETC-only was least accurate, followed by linear interpolation, UAV-only, fixed-weight fusion, SQA-TF without quality adaptation, and the full SQA-TF.

Table 4 decomposes the improvement using Eq. (17). Relative to fixed-weight fusion, SQA-TF reduced the six error metrics by 29.4–32.9%. Part of this reduction is already obtained by SQA-TF without quality adaptation, which differs from fixed-weight fusion through the topology-based mapping, temporal association, and flow-consistency term, and reduces errors by 10.6–12.5%. These three components were not ablated separately, so their individual contributions cannot be distinguished. Adding quality weighting reduced the errors by a further 21.0–23.5% relative to the model without it. Relative to UAV-only estimation, the full method reduced errors by 41.2–43.4%. The reductions refer to different baselines and are not additive.

sec.p: The effect of quality weighting was similar for the three variables (21.0–23.5%), although only the UAV residual for a given cell contains all three variables directly and the ETC constraint acts on speed alone. Through the flow-consistency and smoothness terms, a change in the estimated speed field also alters flow and density, which is consistent with the similar reductions. For each comparison in Table 4, the relative reductions in MAE and RMSE were similar.

sec.title: 5.2. Variability across trials
sec.p: Figure 4 and Figure 5 show the flow MAE and density MAE of each method in each of the 200 trials. The separation between methods in Table 3 holds in individual trials: the SQA-TF curve lies below the curves of all other methods throughout, and in most trials the errors of SQA-TF without quality adaptation lie below those of fixed-weight fusion. The trial-to-trial spread of SQA-TF is also narrower than that of the single-source methods and linear interpolation; its flow MAE remains mostly between about 70 and 100 veh/h/lane, whereas the ETC-only flow MAE ranges from about 135 to 230 veh/h/lane. Single-source estimation is thus both less accurate and less stable across realisations of the observations.

sec.title: 5.3. Temporal tracking at a representative cell
sec.p: Figure 3, Figure 6, and Figure 7 show the estimated speed, density, and flow at a representative cell over 200 consecutive windows, which include a congestion episode between approximately windows 90 and 135. In this episode, the speed falls to about 50 km/h, density rises to about 50 veh/km/lane, and flow falls to about 1,100–1,200 veh/h/lane. All methods reproduce the overall course of the episode. The methods differ mainly in window-to-window noise: the ETC-only and linear-interpolation estimates fluctuate most, with deviations of about 10 km/h in speed and of several hundred vehicles per hour in flow between adjacent windows, while the SQA-TF estimate follows a smoother path through the congestion onset, minimum, and recovery. The ETC-only flow estimate also lies systematically below the other estimates during the first 30 windows. Because the reference curve is drawn beneath the estimates in these figures, the time-series plots support comparisons of noise and trend between methods but not a visual assessment of lag relative to the reference.

caption.title: Density estimates at a representative cell over 200 time windows
Flow estimates at a representative cell over 200 time windows

sec.title: 5.4. Spatial reconstruction along the corridor
sec.p: Figure 2 and Figure 8 show the speed and density profiles along the corridor, averaged over the 200 trials. All methods locate the three congested sections near km 32, km 77, and km 119. The ETC-only profile departs most from the others: it places the speed minima several kilometres per hour lower, most visibly in the section near km 77 where its minimum is about 48 km/h against about 53 km/h for the remaining methods, and it underestimates free-flow speed beyond about km 100. This bias is consistent with the use of interval constraints alone: a travel time fixes the harmonic mean speed over an interval of several kilometres, and without local information the regularisation spreads the delay of a short congested section over neighbouring cells. In the density profile, the differences between methods are smaller than in the speed profile and are concentrated near the three density peaks of about 31, 49, and 40 veh/km/lane.

caption.title: Density profile along the corridor (means over 200 simulation trials)

sec.p: Figure 9 resolves the error by cell. For speed and density, the largest errors of ETC-only and linear interpolation occur between roughly km 60 and km 110, the section that contains the most severe congestion, while the flow errors of linear interpolation are high along most of the corridor. The errors of SQA-TF are low and nearly uniform along the corridor for all three variables, and those of SQA-TF without quality adaptation and fixed-weight fusion are intermediate.

caption.title: MAE of speed, density, and flow by cell along the corridor for the six methods (200 simulation trials)

sec.title: 6. Discussion
sec.p: The results support two conclusions about the design of UAV–ETC fusion. First, ETC travel times are informative but insufficient on their own: ETC-only estimation was the least accurate method for every variable, and its errors concentrated in the congested section where a single interval contains both free-flowing and queued traffic. This pattern follows from the measurement itself. A travel time constrains only the sum of cell traversal times along an interval, so many local speed profiles are compatible with one observation, and the regularisation cannot recover a short bottleneck without local data. The gain of the fused methods over both single-source methods confirms the complementarity assumed in Section 1. It is also consistent with the field comparison of Kessler et al. [19], in which travel-time data contributed to speed reconstruction only when integrated as travel times rather than converted to local speeds. Error magnitudes from that and other field studies [21], [22] are not compared with the present values, because they refer to different corridors, sensors, and reference data.

Quality weighting produced the largest single step in Table 4: with the corridor, the observation model, and all other components unchanged, it reduced the six error measures by 21.0–23.5% relative to the same model with fixed weights. Without weighting, a low-quality UAV measurement or a widely dispersed set of ETC travel times pulls the estimate as strongly as a reliable observation; scaling each residual by its quality score reduces that pull without discarding the observation. The size of the gain depends on how closely the quality scores track the actual observation errors. In the simulation, this relationship is set by the data generator, so Table 4 measures the gain for that relationship only. The effect of errors in the quality scores was not tested.

The spatial analysis shows where the method is most useful. The largest speed and density errors of ETC-only estimation and interpolation occurred in the section containing the main congestion episode, where a single gantry interval contains both free-flowing and queued traffic, and this is also where SQA-TF reduced errors most (Figure 9). A UAV observation inside such an interval can locate a queue that the gantry-to-gantry travel time cannot resolve, whereas in free-flowing sections the methods differ less. For a highway operator, this suggests directing UAV flights to intervals with recurrent bottlenecks and relying on ETC data elsewhere. The experiment used a single coverage pattern, so the relative merits of alternative flight plans remain untested.

Several limitations bound these conclusions. The evaluation used synthetic data; detection, tracking, and record-matching errors were represented only through the synthetic observation errors, and no field validation against independent measurements was performed. The comparison did not include established fusion methods such as adaptive smoothing [17], the fusion scheme of van Lint and Hoogendoorn [18], Kalman filtering [8], or Physics-Informed Deep Learning (PIDL) [11], [12]; the baselines therefore show that SQA-TF improves on simpler alternatives, not that it outperforms the state of the art. The influence of cell length, window length, and UAV coverage ratio on accuracy was not analysed, and the topology mapping, temporal association, and flow-consistency term were evaluated only jointly. ETC gantry counts were not used as flow observations, although they could constrain flow directly at gantry cross-sections. Finally, computational cost was not reported, which matters for online use on long corridors.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: ETC and UAV measurements resolve different features of highway traffic. A gantry pair records the time needed to traverse an interval. A UAV can locate a queue within that interval, but only during the part of the flight when the queue is visible. SQA-TF uses the former as a path constraint and the latter as a local observation.

Across 200 trials, SQA-TF gave a speed MAE of 4.12 km/h, compared with 5.37 km/h for the same model with fixed observation weights and 6.14 km/h for fixed-weight fusion. Flow and density followed the same ordering. The spatial profiles locate the largest errors of ETC-only estimation and interpolation in the interval group containing the most severe congestion.

The simulation quantifies the improvement for one corridor geometry and one observation design. Its operational relevance depends on whether video and gantry quality indicators can identify unreliable measurements in service. Independent speed and density measurements at both covered and uncovered sites would allow that assumption to be tested.
